extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor attorneys, human resources professionals, platform companies, labor organizations, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation guidance for the 'control' factor of the FLSA economic reality test used to determine independent contractor vs. employee status, including specific considerations such as use of technology, price-setting, and the ability to work for others. The page explains how these considerations should be weighed and gives illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology to supervise the performance of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant consideration is not simply the employer's use of technology to supervise, but the use of technology 'to supervise the performance of the work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only forms of technology deployed by the employer as a means of supervising the performance of the work are probative of economic dependence. The Department rejected a blanket exclusion of technology from the analysis and likewise rejected treating all workplace technology as automatically probative. Focus on whether technology is specifically deployed to supervise or direct how the worker performs their job.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over prices or rates for goods or services
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether 'the employer controls economic aspects of the working relationship . . . including control over prices or rates for services.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an entity other than the worker sets a price or rate for the goods or services offered by the worker, or the worker accepts a predetermined price or rate without meaningful ability to negotiate it, this is evidence favoring employee status. Workers in business for themselves generally can set or negotiate prices. Presence of a contract stating prices does not automatically determine status; analyze the worker's ability to negotiate or alter contract terms. The Department will not predetermine the weight of this consideration; it is one fact among others in a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker's ability to set or negotiate prices
rubrics_metrics.description: A worker's ability to negotiate or set prices for services indicates they are more likely in business for themself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: testimony that installers could negotiate prices directly with customers and keep the money supported a finding of business control. Conversely, being 'regimented under one organization' and receiving compensation the organization dictates supports employee status. Ability to set prices can also appear in contracts between a business and an independent contractor—but the practical ability to negotiate and change prices is what matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information asymmetry regarding pricing (captured under economic aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of access to pricing information may prevent a worker from negotiating prices that would further their business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to adopt 'information asymmetry' as a separate criterion because it is ambiguous, but agrees the concept is captured by the broader inquiry into employer control of economic aspects. Evidence that an employer conceals pricing data or otherwise withholds information that precludes negotiation may be probative of employee status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions taken solely to comply with specific law or regulation are not indicative of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions taken by the potential employer for the sole purpose of complying with a specific, applicable Federal, State, Tribal, or local law or regulation are not indicative of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulatory text will state this exclusion. However, where a business goes beyond mere compliance in ways that serve the business's own compliance methods (e.g., onerous approval/monitoring systems imposed on workers at their expense), those extra steps may be indicative of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to work for others (employer limitations and worker freedoms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the employer 'explicitly limits the worker's ability to work for others' or 'places demands on workers' time that do not allow them to work for others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control over the ability to work for others can be exercised directly (contractual prohibition) or indirectly (demands on time, scheduling, financial penalties, onerous approval systems). The mere fact that a worker can or does work for others is not dispositive of independent contractor status—multiple jobs or 'multi-apping' may reflect economic necessity rather than business independence. Examine whether the freedom to work reflects true economic independence or masks economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect restrictions on working for others (time, restrictions, monetary or procedural barriers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect means of limiting workers' ability to work for others—such as making demands on time, imposing restrictions, requiring complex approvals, or imposing financial penalties—are relevant to the control inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department revised regulatory text to capture not only demands on time but also 'restrictions' that effectively preclude work for others. Examples include systems so complex and onerous that they make working for other carriers impracticable, monitoring requirements a worker must pay for, or platform practices that coerce continuous acceptance of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer control via pay structures or bonus systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Control exercised through pay structures (including bonus pay systems) that influence worker behavior is relevant to the control factor as part of employer control of economic aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged explicit attention to pay structures used by platform companies to coerce more work. The Department considers such arrangements captured by inquiry into employer control of 'economic aspects of the working relationship.' These arrangements may be probative of control depending on the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor is determinative; totality-of-the-circumstances test
rubrics_metrics.description: The control factor—and any single consideration within it—is not determinative by itself; the economic reality test is a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis where no one factor is dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to predetermine weights for factors. Price-setting, supervision, ability to work for others, and other considerations are each one piece of evidence. Courts adapt analysis to the particular working relationship, workplace, and industry. More indicia of worker control favors independent contractor status, but must be considered together with opportunity for profit/loss, investment, permanence, skill, and other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap and distinct perspectives of related factors (price in control vs. opportunity for profit/loss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of price-setting appears both under the 'control' factor (employer actions that control economic aspects) and the 'opportunity for profit or loss' factor (ways the individual has opportunities for profit or loss based on managerial skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that discussing price in both contexts is appropriate because each factor approaches price from a different analytical angle. This is not improper double counting; instead, each factor considers different facets of pricing as they relate to control and entrepreneurial opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrative example: Nature and degree of control (employee vs. independent contractor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts showing the employer sets schedules, determines work location, prohibits working for others, and supervises staff indicate employee status; facts showing the worker markets services, sets their own prices, lacks supervision, and works for multiple clients indicate independent contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example A (Alpha House nurse): employer-set schedule, internal policies prohibiting other nursing-home employment, supervisory check-ins—indicate employee status. Example B (Beta House therapist): marketing via website, sets prices, no supervision, works for multiple nursing homes—indicate independent contractor status. Use such fact-focused comparisons to apply the control factor within the totality test.
